artist.name: Joelyn
artist.intro: An evolving space for paintings, small observations, and stories told in color.
bio: I’m Joelyn. This is a space for exploring color, noticing the everyday, and finding a little poetry in ordinary things.
A changing sky, a flower on the table, a face in a quiet moment — each offers a starting point. The work begins with looking, and leaves room for feeling.

This portfolio currently uses credited public-domain paintings as a demo collection, alongside sample journal writing and a stock studio photograph. Personal artwork and a full artist biography can take their place as the collection grows.
artist.statement: To make room for the ordinary. To follow the light. To let a painting hold a moment a little longer.

journal.title: On looking slowly
journal.excerpt: What changes when we give a painting — or an ordinary afternoon — a little more of our time.

image.alt: Pink water lilies float across green and blue pond reflections, with broad ochre, violet, and turquoise brushstrokes filling the canvas.

credit.label: Claude Monet · Art Institute of Chicago / Wikimedia Commons

body.text: A painting rarely gives everything away at once. The first glance finds the largest shape, the brightest color, perhaps a familiar subject. Then the eye begins its quieter work. It follows a line, notices a patch of blue, returns to something it almost missed.

There is pleasure in allowing that second look. Without needing to name every brushstroke, we can simply notice how the surface changes as we move through it. A color that seemed green from a distance becomes gold, violet, and turquoise up close.
Give the eye somewhere to wander

In Monet’s Water Lily Pond, the usual anchors of a landscape fall away. There is no clear horizon to divide earth from sky. Reflections move across the canvas, and small pink flowers give the eye a place to rest before it wanders again. Looking at it feels less like reading a scene and more like following the light.

Try staying with one part of a painting for a moment. Notice its edges: sharp in one place, nearly lost in another. Then look at the space around it. The shapes you first treated as background may begin to feel just as present as the subject.
Attention is a kind of space we can give to things.
Carry that attention outside

The same practice belongs to ordinary days. A shadow moves across a table. Leaves change color when the clouds pass. A glass of water holds a small, moving picture of the room. None of these things asks for an answer. They ask only to be seen.
It can help to choose one small observation and stay with it for a minute. There is no need to photograph it, turn it into a painting, or make it useful. Some moments can remain moments.
This is a sample journal entry. The featured image is Claude Monet’s Water Lily Pond, 1917–19, from the Art Institute of Chicago’s public-domain collection.

journal.title: A palette for quiet moments
journal.excerpt: Earth, rose, green, and a little blue: a few thoughts on color that leaves room to breathe.

image.alt: An overflowing bouquet of orange, yellow, and white chrysanthemums in a brown vase on a blue-green patterned tablecloth.

credit.label: Pierre-Auguste Renoir · Art Institute of Chicago / Wikimedia Commons

body.text: A quiet palette does not have to be a pale one. Deep greens, warm ochres, and a touch of red can sit together without raising their voices. Often the feeling comes from the relationship between colors, rather than from any single color on its own.

Look at the flowers in Renoir’s Chrysanthemums. There is so much warmth in the orange and cream petals, but it is the blue-green cloth beneath them that lets the bouquet breathe. The cooler field gives each warm mark a little more presence.
Begin with a relationship

Instead of starting with a list of favorite colors, begin with a pair: warm and cool, light and dark, soft and clear. Add one color, then notice what happens to the other. A brown can look almost violet beside ochre; a muted green can feel bright against a dusty rose.

A small page of color studies is a useful place to explore. Let each patch touch another. Try the same color beside three different neighbors. There is no finished picture to worry about, only a series of small discoveries.
Sometimes the most expressive color is the one that makes room for another.
Leave a little room

A painting needs places where the eye can pause. That might be a broad area of a single color, a softened edge, or a quieter passage between two busy shapes. Restraint makes the livelier marks feel more alive.

The palette can also begin outside the studio: a dry leaf against a blue pavement, a cream wall beside a wooden door, the pink underside of a flower. These small arrangements are already doing the work of composition.
There is no perfect recipe for quiet color. The useful question is simpler: does each color have enough space to be itself, and does it help us see the colors around it?
This is a sample journal entry. The featured image is Pierre-Auguste Renoir’s Chrysanthemums, 1881–82, from the Art Institute of Chicago’s public-domain collection.

journal.title: The space between marks
journal.excerpt: A note on beginnings, imperfect studies, and giving a painting room to find its own shape.

image.alt: A close view of well-used paintbrushes with traces of colorful paint on their wooden handles.

body.text: The blank page can make a beginning feel larger than it is. Before there is an image, there is a decision: which brush, which color, where to place the first mark. It helps to remember that the first mark does not have to explain the whole painting.
A small study offers a gentler beginning. A few shapes, a limited palette, a familiar object on the table. There is enough to respond to, without needing to resolve every detail.
Let the study stay a study

Some paintings begin as questions. What happens if this shadow is cooler? What if the background is as present as the figure? What can be left out? A study can answer one of these questions without becoming a finished work.

The useful part is often the imperfect part: a line that moves in an unexpected way, a mixture that is not quite the intended color, a shape that leaves more space than planned. Looking at these moments with curiosity can be more helpful than correcting them immediately.
A pause can be part of the painting, too.
Step back, then return

Distance changes the picture. Up close, it is easy to become occupied with a single edge. From the other side of the room, the larger relationships return. A small dark mark may have more weight than expected; a busy area may be asking for a quiet neighbor.

Stepping away for a while gives another kind of distance. The work remains where it is, but the eye returns a little differently. It may be easier to see what the painting already has, rather than what we hoped it would become.
There is room for unfinished work in a practice. It records an attempt, a direction, a particular way of seeing on a particular day. Not every beginning has to become a conclusion.
